note: Hand-written script, spoken verbatim. Structure: the arrival lines are one continuous spine (stop 1 introduces her and the walk, stop 6 closes it), each scene carries a single idea, and every tap adds something neither the scene nor another tap has said. A fact appears exactly once in the whole tour. Omitting a hotspot id here deletes that point from the tour.

stop_01_ludgate_hill.arrival: Good morning to you, and welcome. Nell Baker is my name. I sell violets and watercress at the top of Ludgate Hill, and have done these nine years, so I know this road better than I know my own stairs. I am to walk you down it, from here to the river, six stops in all, and tell you what I know as we go. Two things before we set off. When something takes your eye, touch it, and I will tell you what it is; and if you would rather ask me outright, hold the green disc and speak, for I shall hear you well enough. Now then. It is the spring of 1850, and this is Ludgate Hill.

cards.stop_01_ludgate_hill_c1: This hill is at its worst and its best by seven in the morning. Every cart and cab and omnibus on it is carrying something that must be sold before dark, and the drivers know it. I come up the middle of it twice a day with a basket on my hip, and I have learned to step lively. Nobody on Ludgate Hill waits for anybody.
cards.stop_01_ludgate_hill_c2: Stand still a moment and see what the whole street is pointed at. Every roof on both sides steps down and away so that the church has the sky to itself. There is nothing built across this view, nothing over it, and no railway bridge to spoil it. Londoners take that for granted. I never have.

hotspots.stop_01_ludgate_hill_arrival_p1: That is Saint Paul's, and that is where we are going. It stands higher than anything else in this city, so it is how a body finds their way home from any street on this side of the water.
hotspots.stop_01_ludgate_hill_arrival_p2: Sixpence to ride, if you have sixpence. I have not. My money is stock money and it goes on flowers, so I use my own shoes and keep the difference for market.
hotspots.stop_01_ludgate_hill_arrival_p3: That boy is the reason your boots are still fit to be seen. There is no drain in this road, and what the horses leave has to go somewhere. He sweeps you a clean path and stays at it until the light goes.
hotspots.stop_01_ludgate_hill_stop_01_ludgate_hil: See how the stone has gone black on the weather side. That is coal. Every house in London burns it, and the church wears the soot of the whole city like an old coat.
The omnibus is the clerk's carriage. Look at the top of it, packed with men who could not afford to be late and would rather sit in the wind than pay for inside.
Brewers' drays go at their own pace and ask nobody's leave. Everything you can see is either pulling a load or getting out of the way of one.
Sir Christopher Wren built that, and it took him the best part of his life; it was counted finished in 1711. Men were born, apprenticed and buried while it went up.
A coffee house, and there will be a stall on the pavement beside it before five in the morning. Half the trades in this street begin work before there is light to see by.
Watch how it takes the middle of the road and dares the rest to argue. The hill is steep enough that the horses walk it, and everything behind must walk it too.

stop_01_ludgate_hill.transitionOut: Come along with me now, up past the booksellers' windows. I want you to see what stands at the top of this hill, and what has grown up hard against it.

stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard.arrival: Here we are, and here is my pitch. You may have thought a cathedral would keep a quiet green about it. Not this one. Trade comes right up to the railings: drapers, booksellers, milliners, chemists, all shouldering in as close as they are let. I stand at the corner because the crowd is thickest here, and a crowd is the whole of my living.

cards.stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_c1: I am at Farringdon market by four in the morning to buy. A shilling buys me a dozen bunches wholesale, and I sell them on at a penny each, if they keep their sweetness and if it does not rain. That is the whole of my trade. Some days it comes home. Some days I carry it back in the basket, dead weight.
cards.stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_c2: Look how the shop fronts press against the church, sign above sign. For two hundred years this yard was where England bought its books, and the trade has never gone away; it only moved a street back and carried on. There is more paper sold within a hundred paces of us than anywhere in the kingdom.

hotspots.stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_arrival_p1: The clock inside empties into the street. When service ends, the doors open and my corner is worth standing at, and when it is over I might as well be selling to the pigeons.
hotspots.stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_arrival_p2: A tea merchant, and behind that window a counting house. Every one of these has clerks who come out at noon with a few coppers and no idea what to do with them, which suits me very well.
hotspots.stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_arrival_p3: That is my stock, and it must be sold today. Flowers keep no better than fish. What is sweet this morning is rubbish tomorrow, and there is no putting it by.
hotspots.stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_stop_02_st_p: By ten on a bad morning you can lose the whole of that dome in the smoke, dome, cross and all, standing where I stand now. It comes back at noon if the wind is kind.
Violets sell to gentlemen going in to dine and to young men who have done something they are sorry for. I can tell the second sort at twenty paces.
The shops will buy my watercress themselves if it looks big and fresh, and a shopkeeper pays quicker than a crowd. Cress is a breakfast, so it must be sold before eight or not at all.
Booksellers, and behind them printers, and behind them the men who carry it. A book you buy in the country was likely made within a quarter mile of this railing.
That lad is carrying somebody's whole day in his arms. Boys like him are the post of this quarter; they go faster than a cart and cost less than a horse.

stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard.transitionOut: Now come round the back of the church with me, into the narrowest street in the City. You will smell the paper before you see it.

stop_03_paternoster_row.arrival: Paternoster Row. It is barely a street; in places two carts fill the whole width of it, and the houses stand up so tall on either hand that the daylight has to be sent for. Behind every one of those windows somebody is printing, binding, or selling what is printed. This is where the words come from.

cards.stop_03_paternoster_row_c1: There is scarce room here for any other trade. Booksellers and publishers took the Row long ago and have kept it, and what you see on the pavement is not customers but porters: parcels going out to every town in England, and coming back again when they do not sell.
cards.stop_03_paternoster_row_c2: Mind yourself against the wall when a cart comes through, for there is nowhere else to go. These little courts running off the Row are not decoration; they are the way out when the street is choked, and every porter in the quarter knows them better than the Row itself.
cards.stop_03_paternoster_row_c4: Now that is the whole business made plain. One man reads and the rest lean in. There is a new weekly out this spring called Household Words, twopence the number, and twopence will serve a dozen listeners if one of them has his letters. That is how news reaches people like me: aloud, and second hand.

hotspots.stop_03_paternoster_row_arrival_p1: The church is directly behind these roofs, not a hundred paces off. The Row lives in its shadow and always has; that is how it came by its name, from the prayer, said by folk walking round the church.
hotspots.stop_03_paternoster_row_arrival_p2: Every sign along here says the same thing in a different name. When one trade takes a street entire, the rents follow it, and no baker or butcher can afford to stand among them.
hotspots.stop_03_paternoster_row_arrival_p3: Handcarts, not wagons. A wagon cannot turn in the Row, so the paper goes out by hand as far as the wide streets, and is loaded properly there.
hotspots.stop_03_paternoster_row_stop_03_paternos: A publisher's board. The man whose name is on it never touches the paper; he pays the printer, pays the binder, and takes the risk of the whole edition on his own head.
Those men carry loads that would put me on my knees, and they do it at a trot. Ask any of them what is in the parcel and he will tell you he has not opened one in his life.
Through that arch is a court, and through the court is the Churchyard. The whole quarter is stitched together with such holes in the wall, and a stranger would never find one.
Lovell's Court. Courts like this hold a printing house or two apiece, tucked out of sight, and the noise of the presses comes up out of them like something breathing.
Two of them, and the street is full. When a cart stops here to unload, everything behind it stops as well, and there is a good deal said about it.
He is not showing off. Plenty standing there cannot read a line, and would sooner hear it read than own the paper, so a man with a clear voice is never short of company.
Twopence for a number, mind, when a loaf of bread stands at more than fivepence. Reading is cheap now in a way it never was, and that is newer than you would think.

stop_03_paternoster_row.transitionOut: Enough of print for one morning. We go west from here, where the road widens and the traffic doubles. Keep close to me, and I will show you something that is not there at all.

stop_04_fleet_street.arrival: Fleet Street, and that arch ahead is Temple Bar, the old gate of the City. Everything going in or out of London this way must squeeze under it, which is why nothing here moves faster than a walk. And there is a river beneath your feet. The Fleet runs under this road, covered over, all the way down to the Thames.

cards.stop_04_fleet_street_c1: A coffee stall does its best trade at either end of the day, in the dark before work and the dark after it. A penny the mug, a halfpenny the half. For a good many people standing at that stall, that is breakfast, and there will be nothing else until night.
cards.stop_04_fleet_street_c2: The Bar is not there for show. It marks where the City begins, and even the Queen must stop at it and ask leave before she comes through. The rest of us do not ask; we simply wait our turn, which takes longer.
cards.stop_04_fleet_street_c4: Last year the cholera came through London and the City alone buried three thousand seven hundred and sixty three. The doctors said it was the bad air that carried it, so we all learned to fear a smell. The Fleet runs under that grating, and everything this street pours away goes down with it.

hotspots.stop_04_fleet_street_arrival_p1: Sir Christopher had that built too, after the Fire, and it has been narrowing this road ever since. There is talk of pulling it down for the traffic, and there has been talk of it my whole life.
hotspots.stop_04_fleet_street_arrival_p2: Stalls like that will stand all night here. Printers work while the town sleeps, and printers must eat, so there is always something hot to be had in Fleet Street at three in the morning.
hotspots.stop_04_fleet_street_arrival_p3: Put your ear near one of those gratings after rain and you will hear it. There is a whole river down there in the dark, running under the shops as if nothing had happened to it.
hotspots.stop_04_fleet_street_stop_04_fleet_stree: Bread and butter at the stall, cut thin, and a slice of my watercress laid on it if I have any left. That is what a working breakfast looks like standing up.
Under that arch is the boundary. On this side the City has its own constables and its own rules; a step through and you are in Westminster's world, and the law changes with the paving.
A coffee house where the papers are taken and read by anyone who buys a cup. That is Fleet Street entire: print above, news below, and something hot in between.
The omnibus must go under with an inch to spare, and the men riding on the roof duck without being told. They have all done it a hundred times.
A cab is for people whose time is worth more than their money. There are more of them on this street than any other I know, because a newspaper man is always late.
My flowers do a kindness here beyond selling. A bunch of violets held under the nose is what a lady does when she must walk past a grating in July.
Beyond the Bar the road runs on to Westminster and the Parliament house. What we tip into the Fleet goes down to the river, and the river goes past their windows too. They will find that out.

stop_04_fleet_street.transitionOut: Now come down toward the water with me. Where the Fleet gives out into the Thames there is a bridge, and from the middle of it you can see what this city truly runs on.

stop_05_blackfriars.arrival: Blackfriars Bridge. Stand at the parapet a minute and look both ways at once: carts on the stone above, boats on the water below, and the gas works over the far side making the smoke that hangs on all of it. The Thames is not scenery. It is the busiest road in England, and it never closes.

cards.stop_05_blackfriars_c1: The steamers changed everything within my own memory. A halfpenny or a penny for a short reach upriver, twopence for further, and you are there before a cab has cleared the Strand. Half the men you see going to work on that water once walked it.
cards.stop_05_blackfriars_c2: This is old Blackfriars still, Mr Mylne's bridge of Portland stone, opened in 1769, with nine low arches carrying the whole of this traffic. It has stood eighty years and it shows every one of them; they say the stone is wearing and it will have to come down.
cards.stop_05_blackfriars_c4: Look over the side at the boys down there in the mud. They are waiting on the tide, not on the boats. When the water goes out it leaves the whole floor of the river open to anybody bold enough to walk on it, and there is always somebody bold enough.

hotspots.stop_05_blackfriars_arrival_p1: The penny steamers run to a timetable, which is a new thing on this river. A waterman went when he had a fare; the steamer goes whether you are aboard or not.
hotspots.stop_05_blackfriars_arrival_p2: Everything crosses here: droves of beasts going to market, brewers' carts, cabs, and folk on foot keeping to the sides. The bridge earns its keep from before dawn until well after dark.
hotspots.stop_05_blackfriars_arrival_p3: Gas works. That smoke is what lights the shop windows and the street lamps you will walk home by, and it is made on the riverbank because the coal comes in by water.
hotspots.stop_05_blackfriars_stop_05_blackfriars_: She is carrying more people in one trip than a wherry could carry in a day, and she does not care which way the tide runs. That is the whole of it, in one boat.
Those stairs are how you get from the road down to the water, and they are older than the bridge. Every set of river stairs has its own watermen who count it theirs.
Wherries, waiting. A waterman rows a licensed boat and served seven years to learn it, and the steam is taking his living from him while he sits there. It is a trade going out in front of us.
Carriages down the middle, foot folk to the sides, and no rail between. You learn to walk close to the parapet and not to think about it.
Nine arches, and the water goes through them faster than it looks. Watermen call shooting a bridge the quickest way to drown on purpose, and they are not entirely joking.
Wharves, works and warehouses, all of them burning coal on the water's edge because that is where the coal arrives. The river feeds the smoke and the smoke settles back on the river.
Mudlarks. Coal first, then bones, rope and bits of iron, and every piece of it sold on to somebody who asks no questions. A middling day comes to threepence.
Even up here the cab must give way to a drove of sheep. London still walks its dinner to market on the hoof, straight over this bridge and into the City.

stop_05_blackfriars.transitionOut: Come down the stairs with me now, careful as you go. I want you to finish where everything in this city ends up.

stop_06_thames_foreshore.arrival: Mind your footing. This is the foreshore at low water, and it is the bottom of London in every sense. Everything the town drops, loses or pours away arrives here twice a day when the tide goes out, and there are people whose whole living is waiting for it.

cards.stop_06_thames_foreshore_c1: Those children are working, not playing. They come down at the ebb and go over the mud barefoot, because boots are worth more than what they will find and cannot be spared to the ooze. Glass and nails are the usual pay for carelessness, and there is nothing to be done for a cut but keep going.
cards.stop_06_thames_foreshore_c2: This is the working front of the greatest church in England: stairs, chains, piles, barges nosing in on the tide. Coal for the city comes up on this water, and the men who unload it will never once be asked into the building on the hill above them.
cards.stop_06_thames_foreshore_c4: A basket like mine will hold whatever sells. Violets in the spring, oranges when the flowers are done, watercress the year round, and I have carried all three in this one. That is my whole security, and it is the same security as theirs down there: what you can carry, and whether anybody wants it today.

hotspots.stop_06_thames_foreshore_arrival_p1: From up on the hill that dome belongs to the bishops and the bankers. From down here in the mud it is the same dome, and it looks at us just the same. I have always liked that about it.
hotspots.stop_06_thames_foreshore_arrival_p2: She was run aground on purpose at high water, so the men could unload her straight onto the shore with no wharf to pay for and no crane to wait on. The flood will lift her off again this evening, none the worse.
hotspots.stop_06_thames_foreshore_arrival_p3: Those steps are green with weed to the waterline, and that mark is where the tide will be again by evening. Do not go below it, and do not turn your back on the river.
hotspots.stop_06_thames_foreshore_stop_06_thames_: Every set of stairs like this has its own crew of children, and they do not trespass on each other. There is more law among them down here than you would suppose.
Coal is what they hope for, fallen from the barges. A gentleman wrote all this down last year, going about asking such children what they earned. It was in the newspaper, and nothing changed.
Wharf stairs, and slick as glass at the ebb. The river gives you two hours at the bottom of the tide and takes them back without asking whether you are finished.
Chains and timber piles hold the landing to its work while the barges strain against them. Every bit of iron you can see down here is worth money to somebody, which is why so little of it is loose.
She will lie in the ooze until the water comes back for her, and the mud will be turned over twice before that by the children. Nothing is left on this shore for long.
Wicker, mended twice, and it will outlast the shawl. A basket is the one tool of my trade, and I would sooner lose a day's stock than lose it.

stop_06_thames_foreshore.transitionOut: And that is the end of it, down here in the mud where everything the city drops comes to rest. You have seen the top of the hill and the bottom of the river in one morning, and there is not much of London that is not somewhere between the two. I am Nell Baker. I shall be at the top of Ludgate Hill tomorrow at five, with whatever is fresh. Mind those steps going up, they are slick as glass. And thank you kindly for walking with me.
